To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the response of body weight gain to fat supplementation was greater at 27 than 10 C, that the response to glucose was greater at 10 than 27 C, that the responses of feed efficiency and carcass fat were similar at both temperatures and that the response of feed efficiency and body weight gain to dietary fat was greater than to dietary carbohydrates.

the responses of body weight gain and carcass fat to dietary energy sources were influenced by temperature and that the responses of weight gain to dietary fat were more pronounced at the high environmental temperature.

1) dietary fat and glucose are equally effective in increasing weight gain and feed conversion of turkeys kept either at 10 C or at 27 C; 2) the response of weight gain and conversion to fat is temperature dependent, being greater at 27 C than at 10 C; and 3) carcass fat was increased more at 10 C than at 27 C by dietary fat or glucose.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interaction between environmental temperature and energy sources on growth performance of turkeys.
the effect of dietary energy sources on the performance of turkeys.
the effects of dietary fat and carbohydrate on the performance of turkeys.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
dietary carbohydrates and fat have differential effects on growth performance and carcass fat of turkeys depending on the environmental temperature.
the response to dietary energy sources and environmental temperatures is dependent upon mode and level of dietary energy addition and the response criteria.
turkeys kept at 27 C respond more to dietary fat supplementation than to dietary glucose supplementation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
dietary fat supplementation is more effective in increasing growth and efficiency and carcass fat deposition at 27 C than at 10 C, whereas the reverse was true for glucose-energy.
turkeys are able to adjust their metabolism to environmental temperature and dietary composition.

the response of body weight gain, feed utilization, and carcass lipid to dietary fat or carbohydrates was more sensitive to environmental temperature when fat or carbohydrates were added isocalorically or at the expense of fiber.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the responses of weight gain, feed conversion efficiency, and carcasses fat to dietary fat and carbohydrates vary with temperature.
the effect of dietary energy source on growth and carcass fat was dependent on the temperature at which the birds were kept.

the effect of environmental temperature on the responses of turkeys to dietary energy sources varies depending on the dietary energy source and on whether the energy source is given in excess of energy requirements or isocalorific.
